scenes.narration: You type a website name. But computers only talk in numbers. D N S is the phone book that connects the two.

scenes.heading: The phone book and the operator
scenes.narration: Say you want to call Alice, but you only know her name. You look her up in a phone book and find her number. D N S does exactly that for websites. Your computer asks a helper called the resolver, and the resolver does the legwork. It asks the root servers, then the top level domain servers, then the one that really knows. Finally it hands the number back, and remembers it for a while.

items.story: Root, then TLD, then the expert

scenes.heading: Setting it up on a router
scenes.narration: On a Cisco router, two commands turn D N S on. One enables lookups. The other tells the router which server to ask.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. Your computer does not ask the root server directly. It asks its resolver. D N S is not U D P only, because big answers and zone transfers use T C P. And the T T L is set by the authoritative server, not by the resolver.

items.wrong: The client asks the root server directly
items.right: It asks its resolver, which does the walking
Large replies and zone transfers use TCP

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. D N S turns names into I P addresses. Resolvers do the hard work, and cache the answers. It uses port fifty-three, mostly U D P. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva DNS lab.

points.t: DNS turns names into IP addresses
Resolvers do the work and cache answers
